newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - Dlr to settle down amid holiday spirit.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Dlr to settle down amid holiday spirit.

text.p: The dollar is likely to trade within a tight range in the near term as major players have started to pull out of the market ahead of the Christmas holiday, analysts said.
However, analysts also cautioned that the thinning volume may result in some unexpected volatility.
"A lot of people are pulling out, which means thin volume, and that always brings the possibility of volatility," noted Scott Siller, senior analyst at MCM CurrencyWatch.
Siller did not expect the dollar to break out of its range versus the major foreign currencies before January.

Commenting on the dollar's rebound after a marked slide on Friday, Siller pointed out dollar/mark posted a "lackluster performance compared to dollar/Swiss, though dollar/Swiss has yet to really break out."

"We are not seeing a dollar/mark recovery like with dollar/Swiss or dollar/yen. It's so hard to figure out what this market wants to do," Siller said who put dollar/mark's next resistance at 1.5585, the high after Friday's slide.
"Dollar/Swiss could continue higher as there is a 19-month bull channel from May 21, 1995, at 1.3470 Swiss francs," the MCM CurrencyWatch analyst added.

Siller was more upbeat on the dollar/yen outlook where he saw room for an attack on a solid resistance level at 114.75 yen, based on "connecting the peaks of 114.92 on October 29 and the high of 114.40 on December 2."
However, this would first require taking out 113.60/70 yen -- or a 62 percent retracement from Friday's slide.
An analyst at a money center bank saw a chance of fresh strength ahead for sterling -- provided the $166 level can be taken out in the near term.
"The $1.66 level is possibly pivotal to decide whether there'll be a fresh down move or not," he said.
Like Siller, that analyst expected more range trading and little action in store until after the New Year.
One factor that experts agreed may affect the dollar is the performance of U.S. financial assets -- mainly stocks.
They warned that a sharp correction in U.S. equities, particularly if accompanied by pressure on Treasury bonds, could lead investors to get out of U.S. financial assets and thus sell the dollar.
